sources.citation: Legère, Karsten (supported by Rainer Vossen). 2017. ISO 639-3 Change Request 2017-017: retire [mwx] Mediak. SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Identity statement only: 'Mediak is a clan name similar to Mosiro and Kisankasa according to Maguire (1948: 7-8) and not a glossonym. Against this background and for linguistic reasons Rottland & Vossen (1977: 226-230) shift all three clans to Akie' (p. 2); 'the claim that Mediak is a distinct language from others also called Dorobo: such as Kisankasa [kqh], Mosiro [mwy], Aasax [aas] doesn't make sense' (p. 3).

sources.citation: Maguire, R. A. J. 1948 [1928]. Il-Torobo. Tanganyika Notes and Records 25: 1-27 (reprint of Journal of the Royal African Society 27 (1928): 127-141, 249-268).
sources.note: The only primary source that names Kisankasa. Ethnographic notes plus a comparative wordlist of 'the Mósiro and Aramanik languages' (pp. 19-22). Kisankasa appears only as a Dorobo group name: list of eight Maasai-named Dorobo types incl. '5. Ol-Kisankasai / Il-Kisankasa' (p. 4); 'Il-Mosiro; Il-Médiak; Il-Kisankasa. The three names given above would seem to denote one and the same type of Dorobo. I have been unable to discover any difference between them. Curiously enough, although I have met many Mosiro and Médiak I have, so far, failed to come across an individual calling himself Kisankasa.…

sources.citation: Wikipedia: 'Kisankasa language' (redirect to Ogiek language), 'Kisankasa people', 'Dorobo peoples', 'Ndorobo language', 'Akie language', 'Serengeti-Dorobo language'; Wikidata Q6416409.
sources.note: Context only. 'Kisankasa language' redirects to Ogiek; 'Kisankasa people' gives Ngorongoro District/Mara Region, 4,670 (1987), citing Brenzinger (ed.) 1992/93 and Ethnologue. 'Akie language' summarizes König/Heine/Legère consonants and vowels (vowel length distinctive) but says nothing on tone or stress.
